summary.text:
Tamworth's General Fund has no debt at all, so its General Fund financing cost ratio is negative — minus 30.21% of net revenue stream, because investment income exceeds financing costs. Every pound the council owes is HRA: £63.060m of PWLB at 4.05% over an average 28.73 years, unchanged all year. Our file holds 22 loans totalling £63,060,194, which ties to the pound.

The investment side beat its own budget by a wide margin — average balances of £58.938m at 4.44% against a strategy assumption of £19.0m at 4.0%, and income of £2.6m against £1.6m. Much of that is £23.6m of capital spend re-profiled into 2026/27 sitting as cash.

The property fund story is a cautionary one told plainly: £7.906m invested, £6.786m now, £2.317m of dividends since 2018/19 against a £1.648m valuation decrease. They were forced out of Hermes Federated in August 2025 when it merged into an L&G fund restricted to UK pension schemes — the same event that returned £8.896m in cash to Darlington.

Both meetings are still ahead: Cabinet 20 August and Council 8 September 2026.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the annual report going to Cabinet on 20 August and Council on 8 September. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first. We hold 22 PWLB loans for Tamworth totalling £63,060,194 against the £63.060m in your report — to the pound. Your CFR ties as well: £3.583m General Fund plus £70.443m HRA is £74.027m, and less the £63.060m of borrowing gives the £10.966m of under-funding you state.

Two things stand out and both are worth a member-facing sentence rather than a technical one.

The first is that your General Fund financing cost ratio is negative — minus 30.21% of net revenue stream — because investment income exceeds financing costs. The General Fund has no external debt at all; every pound Tamworth owes is HRA. That is an unusual position and a strong one, and it is the sort of thing that reads as a typo to a member seeing a negative percentage for the first time. It is not.

The second is how far the investment side beat its own strategy. The 2025/26 strategy assumed £19.0m of balances at 4.0%. The actual was an average £58.938m at 4.44%, against 3-month SONIA of 3.94%, producing £2.6m of income against a £1.6m budget. Your own report explains most of it — £23.6m of capital spend re-profiled into 2026/27 sitting as cash. Worth saying plainly, because a £1m favourable variance that is really a timing effect behaves very differently in next year's budget than one that is structural.

On the borrowing side, your note that "no rescheduling was done during the year as the approximate 1% differential between PWLB new borrowing rates and premature repayment rates made rescheduling unviable" is the right test, and we have now read the identical sentence in Portsmouth's and Shropshire's reports. It is also a number that exists every day and that nobody publishes usably. We compute both curves at both daily fixings and price every council's book against the DMO's own formula. On today's curve, notice 314/26, your HRA book sits about £13.4m below par — 16 of the 22 loans, with the six maturing between 2055 and 2062 at 3.48% to 3.51% carrying £9.4m of it. We are not suggesting anything follows from that: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote. Yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

On the property funds — £7.906m invested, £6.786m now, £2.317m of dividends since 2018/19 against a £1.648m valuation decrease — you set that out more honestly than most reports we read. One piece of sector context you may not have: being forced out of Hermes Federated in August 2025 when it merged into an L&G fund limited to UK pension schemes was not just your problem. Darlington was in the same position and took £8.896m back in cash, which it used to repay maturing debt. It is the kind of thing that looks like bad luck from inside one council and turns out to be a shared event.

Your paragraph giving the 31 March certainty rates — 5.04%, 5.28%, 5.72%, 6.29% and 6.08% — matches our own series to the basis point on all five. You are the fifth council to be five for five with us this summer, and you state all four PWLB margins correctly, which a surprising number of reports do not.

Finally, your report says member training was provided in February and further training is planned during 2026/27. That is exactly what our academy is for, and it is free to local authorities until the end of September. Four courses fit Tamworth: Treasury management for councillors, which is written for the meeting this report goes to; HRA treasury & self-financing, since all your debt is HRA; Pooled funds (CCLA, multi-asset) for the property fund position; and PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
